concepts.name: Brønsted-Lowry acids and bases
concepts.statement: Brønsted and Lowry defined acids and bases in terms of the transfer of hydrogen ions: a compound that donates a proton is a Brønsted-Lowry acid, and a compound that accepts a proton is a Brønsted-Lowry base. An acid-base reaction is, thus, the transfer of a proton from a donor to an acceptor.

concepts.name: Conjugate acid-base pairs
concepts.statement: When an acid donates H<sup>+</sup>, the species that remains is its conjugate base, because it reacts as a proton acceptor in the reverse reaction; when a base accepts H<sup>+</sup>, it is converted to its conjugate acid. Every Brønsted-Lowry reaction therefore involves two conjugate pairs.

concepts.name: Writing acid and base ionization equations
concepts.statement: Acid ionization is the reaction of an acid with water to give hydronium ion and the acid’s conjugate base; base ionization is the reaction of a base with water to give hydroxide ion and the base’s conjugate acid. Writing these equations requires identifying which species donates and which accepts the proton.

concepts.name: Amphiprotic species
concepts.statement: Species capable of either donating or accepting protons are called amphiprotic. When such a species is added to water, both its acid and its base equilibria are established at the same time.

concepts.name: Autoionization of water
concepts.statement: Liquid water undergoes autoionization to a very slight extent, and the equilibrium constant for this reaction is the ion-product constant for water, $K_{\text{w}}$. The process is endothermic, so the extent of ionization, and with it $K_{\text{w}}$, increases with temperature.

concepts.name: Calculating ion concentrations in water
concepts.statement: Because the product of the hydronium and hydroxide ion concentrations is fixed by $K_{\text{w}}$, the two are inversely proportional: knowing one gives the other, and in pure water each is the square root of $K_{\text{w}}$.

concepts.name: Brønsted-Lowry acid
concepts.statement: A Brønsted-Lowry acid is a compound that donates a proton (H<sup>+</sup>) to another compound.

concepts.name: Brønsted-Lowry base
concepts.statement: A Brønsted-Lowry base is a compound that accepts a proton (H<sup>+</sup>) from another compound.

concepts.name: Conjugate acid
concepts.statement: The conjugate acid of a base is the species formed when the base accepts a proton.

concepts.name: Conjugate base
concepts.statement: The conjugate base of an acid is the species formed when the acid donates a proton.

concepts.name: Acid ionization
concepts.statement: Acid ionization is the reaction of an acid with water, yielding hydronium ion and the conjugate base of the acid.

concepts.name: Base ionization
concepts.statement: Base ionization is the reaction of a base with water, yielding hydroxide ion and the conjugate acid of the base.

concepts.name: Amphoteric
concepts.statement: An amphoteric species is one that can act as either an acid or a base.

concepts.name: Autoionization
concepts.statement: Autoionization is a reaction between identical species that yields ionic products; for water, two molecules react to give a hydronium ion and a hydroxide ion.

concepts.name: Ion-product constant for water
concepts.statement: The ion-product constant for water, $K_{\text{w}}$, is the equilibrium constant for the autoionization of water, the product of the hydronium and hydroxide ion concentrations; it is 1.0 × 10<sup>−14</sup> at 25 °C.

concepts.name: Acidic, basic, and neutral solutions
concepts.statement: A solution is neutral if it contains equal concentrations of hydronium and hydroxide ions, acidic if it contains a greater concentration of hydronium ions than hydroxide ions, and basic if it contains a lesser one. Since $K_{\text{w}}$ depends on temperature, the pH of a neutral solution does too.

concepts.name: pH and pOH scales
concepts.statement: Hydronium and hydroxide ion concentrations span many orders of magnitude, so they are expressed with the p-function, the negative base-10 logarithm: pH = −log[H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] and pOH = −log[OH<sup>−</sup>]. Each unit of pH is a tenfold change in hydronium ion concentration.

concepts.name: Sum of pH and pOH
concepts.statement: Taking the negative logarithm of the $K_{\text{w}}$ expression shows that the pH and pOH of any aqueous solution sum to p$K_{\text{w}}$, which is 14.00 at 25 °C.

concepts.name: Converting between concentration, pH and pOH
concepts.statement: The definitions of pH and pOH and their sum let us move among [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>], [OH<sup>−</sup>], pH, and pOH; when taking the log of a value, we keep as many decimal places in the result as there are significant figures in the value.

concepts.name: Measuring pH with meters and indicators
concepts.statement: The acidity of a solution is typically assessed by measuring its pH, directly with a pH meter or visually with colored indicators; the pOH is not usually measured, as it is easily calculated from the pH.

concepts.name: Acidic solution
concepts.statement: An acidic solution contains a greater concentration of hydronium ions than hydroxide ions.

concepts.name: Basic solution
concepts.statement: A basic solution contains a lesser concentration of hydronium ions than hydroxide ions.

concepts.name: Neutral solution
concepts.statement: A neutral solution contains equal concentrations of hydronium and hydroxide ions.

concepts.name: pH
concepts.statement: The pH of a solution is the negative base-10 logarithm of its hydronium ion molarity.

concepts.name: pOH
concepts.statement: The pOH of a solution is the negative base-10 logarithm of its hydroxide ion molarity.

concepts.name: Acid and base ionization constants
concepts.statement: The relative strength of an acid or base is the extent to which it ionizes in water, and it is quantified by the equilibrium constant of its ionization, $K_{\text{a}}$ or $K_{\text{b}}$, in which water, being the solvent, does not appear. The larger the constant, the stronger the acid or base.

concepts.name: Percent ionization
concepts.statement: Another measure of the strength of an acid is its percent ionization, the equilibrium hydronium ion concentration divided by the initial acid concentration, times 100. Unlike $K_{\text{a}}$, the percent ionization of a weak acid varies with its initial concentration, decreasing as the concentration increases.

concepts.name: Conjugate pair strengths
concepts.statement: Adding the acid ionization of HA to the base ionization of A<sup>−</sup> gives the autoionization of water, so the product of their constants is $K_{\text{w}}$. The stronger an acid or base, the weaker its conjugate partner, and the conjugate of a strong acid or base has negligible strength.

concepts.name: Leveling effect
concepts.statement: Acids stronger than H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> react completely with water to give H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, and bases stronger than OH<sup>−</sup> react completely to give OH<sup>−</sup>, so in water all such acids and bases appear equally strong. Their differences show up only in a solvent that is a weaker base or acid than water.

concepts.name: Determining Ka or Kb
concepts.statement: Substituting equilibrium concentrations into the ionization constant expression gives $K_{\text{a}}$ or $K_{\text{b}}$ directly; when only the formal concentration and the pH are known, the pH gives the equilibrium [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] and an ICE table gives the rest.

concepts.name: Calculating weak acid or base equilibria
concepts.statement: An ICE table built from the initial concentration and the ionization constant gives the equilibrium concentrations. When the constant is small and the initial concentration large, the change $x$ may be neglected against it, provided $x$ is less than 5% of the initial concentration; otherwise the quadratic equation is solved.

concepts.name: Binary acid strength
concepts.statement: Across a row of the periodic table, the acid strength of binary hydrogen compounds increases with the electronegativity of the nonmetal, because the polarity of the H–A bond increases; down a group, it increases as the H–A bond strength decreases.

concepts.name: Strengths of oxyacids and hydroxy compounds
concepts.statement: In a ternary compound E–O–H, a central atom of low electronegativity makes the E–O bond ionic and the compound a base; a central atom of high electronegativity or high oxidation number draws electron density from the O–H bond and makes the compound an acid. Elements of intermediate electronegativity give amphoteric hydroxides.

concepts.name: Acid ionization constant
concepts.statement: The acid ionization constant, $K_{\text{a}}$, is the equilibrium constant for the ionization of a weak acid; its negative logarithm is p$K_{\text{a}}$.

forms.condition: the ionization HA + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + A⁻ at equilibrium

concepts.name: Base ionization constant
concepts.statement: The base ionization constant, $K_{\text{b}}$, is the equilibrium constant for the ionization of a weak base; its negative logarithm is p$K_{\text{b}}$.

forms.condition: the ionization B + H₂O ⇌ HB⁺ + OH⁻ at equilibrium

concepts.name: Acidic and basic ions in salts
concepts.statement: The ions of a dissolved salt may undergo acid or base ionization with water. Acidic cations are typically the conjugate acids of weak bases, basic anions are the conjugate bases of weak acids, and the conjugates of strong acids and bases, like the group 1 and 2 cations, are inert.

concepts.name: Predicting the acidity of a salt solution
concepts.statement: We consider each ion separately; where a salt contains both an acidic and a basic ion, or a single amphiprotic ion, the solution is acidic or basic according to whether $K_{\text{a}}$ or $K_{\text{b}}$ is the larger.

concepts.name: Calculating the pH of a salt solution
concepts.statement: The ionization constant of a salt’s acidic or basic ion is found from that of its conjugate partner through $K_{\text{a}}\times K_{\text{b}}=K_{\text{w}}$, and the usual ICE approach then gives the equilibrium concentrations and the pH.

concepts.name: Hydrated metal ions as acids
concepts.statement: Many metal ions bond to water molecules to form complex ions such as [Al(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>; the metal draws electron density from the bonded water molecules, weakening their O–H bonds so that they can donate protons. Aside from the group 1 and some group 2 ions, most metal ions undergo acid ionization to some extent.

concepts.name: Polyprotic acids ionize stepwise
concepts.statement: Acids are classified by the number of protons per molecule they can give up: monoprotic, diprotic, triprotic. A polyprotic acid ionizes in steps, one proton at a time, and each successive ionization is less extensive than the one before, so $K_{\text{a1}}>K_{\text{a2}}>K_{\text{a3}}$.

concepts.name: Calculating polyprotic acid concentrations
concepts.statement: If the first ionization constant of a weak diprotic acid is larger than the second by a factor of at least 20, each step may be treated separately: the first gives [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] and the monoanion, and those concentrations feed the second.

concepts.name: Polyprotic bases
concepts.statement: Polyprotic bases accept more than one proton, in steps, and, as for polyprotic acids, each successive base ionization constant is smaller than the one before.

concepts.name: Monoprotic acid
concepts.statement: A monoprotic acid is an acid containing one ionizable hydrogen atom per molecule.

concepts.name: Diprotic acid
concepts.statement: A diprotic acid is an acid containing two ionizable hydrogen atoms per molecule.

concepts.name: Triprotic acid
concepts.statement: A triprotic acid is an acid that contains three ionizable hydrogen atoms per molecule.

concepts.name: Diprotic base
concepts.statement: A diprotic base is a base capable of accepting two protons.

concepts.name: Stepwise ionization
concepts.statement: Stepwise ionization is the process in which an acid is ionized by losing protons sequentially, one at a time.

concepts.name: What a buffer is
concepts.statement: A solution containing appreciable amounts of a weak conjugate acid-base pair is a buffer, and it resists a change in pH when small amounts of a strong acid or a strong base are added.

concepts.name: How buffers work
concepts.statement: The weak acid of the pair neutralizes added hydroxide, converting it to the conjugate base, and the conjugate base neutralizes added hydronium, converting it to the weak acid. The ratio of the two changes only a little, and so does the pH.

concepts.name: Calculating buffer pH
concepts.statement: We first let the added strong acid or base react completely with the buffer component that neutralizes it, find the new concentrations of the two components, and then solve the equilibrium as before.

concepts.name: Buffer capacity
concepts.statement: The buffer capacity is the amount of acid or base that can be added to a given volume of a buffer before its pH changes significantly. A buffer can neutralize only as much acid or base as it has of the conjugate partner that consumes it, so its capacity depends on the amounts of both components; weak acids and their salts suit pHs below 7, and weak bases and their salts suit pHs above 7.

concepts.name: Henderson-Hasselbalch equation
concepts.statement: Rearranging the acid ionization constant expression and taking the negative logarithm gives pH = p$K_{\text{a}}$ + log([A<sup>−</sup>]/[HA]), which relates the pH of a buffer to the $K_{\text{a}}$ of its weak acid and the ratio of the concentrations of the pair; when the two are equal, pH = p$K_{\text{a}}$.

forms.condition: a buffer of the weak acid HA and its conjugate base A⁻

concepts.name: Titration curves and their stages
concepts.statement: A titration curve plots the pH of the sample against the volume of added titrant. Its initial point is set by the acid, the pre-equivalence region by the unreacted acid and its conjugate base, the equivalence point by the products alone, with a drastic rise in pH, and the postequivalence region by the excess titrant.

concepts.name: Calculating pH in a strong acid titration
concepts.statement: Before the equivalence point the excess strong acid sets the pH. At the equivalence point only water and a neutral salt remain, so the pH is 7.00 at 25 °C. Beyond it the excess strong base sets the pH.

concepts.name: Calculating pH in a weak acid titration
concepts.statement: Before any base is added the pH is that of the weak acid; halfway to equivalence the acid and its conjugate base are equal, so pH = p$K_{\text{a}}$; at equivalence the conjugate base alone makes the solution basic; beyond it the excess strong base sets the pH.

concepts.name: How an acid-base indicator works
concepts.statement: An indicator is a weak acid or base whose conjugate forms have different colors, and the perceived color is set by the ratio [In<sup>−</sup>]/[HIn], which the solution pH fixes. The color change is therefore spread over a color-change interval of about two pH units centered near its p$K_{\text{a}}$.

concepts.name: Choosing an indicator for a titration
concepts.statement: A suitable indicator has a color-change interval that falls within the steep, nearly vertical part of the titration curve at the equivalence point, so that its color changes sharply as the equivalence point is passed.

concepts.name: Color-change interval
concepts.statement: The color-change interval of an indicator is the range in pH over which its color change occurs.
